Act as the design sub-agent for this task.

Extend an eval corpus for Twyne, a writing app where five AI editors (ids: devil = sceptic attacking load-bearing claims; angel = patron protecting what works; scholar = evidence and sources; editor = line editing, concision, structure; reader = the target reader's comprehension) read a draft and leave notes pinned to passages. Background on the editors: /home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne/src/utils/personas.ts.

CONTEXT: In a previous round you wrote `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne/evals/app/cases/room.jsonl`: 8 cases with 550 to 900 word drafts, each with 4 to 6 planted features whose `passage` is a verbatim substring of `draftText` (format and rules in `evals/app/cases/README.md`; read both files first and match their style and schema exactly). All of those drafts are under 4,500 characters. The app clamps the draft it shows the editors to 4,500 characters: when `draftText.length > 4500`, the editors see only `draftText.slice(0, 3150)` plus `draftText.slice(-1350)`, and the middle is replaced by "[…draft trimmed for length…]". The eval needs cases where that matters, so it can measure what the editors miss in the middle of a real chapter.

TASK: append exactly 2 new lines to `evals/app/cases/room.jsonl` (keep the existing 8 lines byte-for-byte unchanged), and update `evals/app/cases/README.md` with a short note about long cases and the clamp.
- `room-long-<slug>` cases, 2,200 to 3,000 words each. Pick two different genres not already heavily used, for example a long-form reported feature and a personal-essay chapter or a memoir chapter. Write real, competent-but-imperfect prose, consistent with the existing cases.
- Each case has 7 or 8 plants, positioned deliberately (use the same `plants` schema). At least 2 plants lie entirely within the first 3,000 characters. At least 3 lie entirely in the middle region, starting after character 3,300 and ending before `draftText.length - 1,500`. At least 1 lies entirely within the last 1,300 characters. Cover the same plant kinds as before, and aim plants at every editor across the case, including a `strong-passage` in the middle.
- Every `passage` is 8 to 40 words, appears EXACTLY ONCE in draftText character for character, and uses straight quotes and plain ASCII punctuation.

VALIDATE with a script in /tmp (not in the repo) before finishing: all 10 lines parse; the 8 original lines are unchanged (compare against a copy you save before editing); the word counts are correct; passages are unique and verbatim; and the position rules hold, computed with JavaScript string indices (`draftText.indexOf(passage)`). Print, for each new case, each plant's id, kind, start index, end index, and region (head | middle | tail). Fix anything that fails and re-run until clean. Do not touch any other file, and do not run git commands that change state; other agents share this checkout. Report the validation output.

# App evaluation corpus

Drafts for running the real Twyne editorial room end to end. Every `draftText` is 550 to 900 words (the app refuses editor notes and rubric judgments under 500), counted as `text.trim().split(/\s+/).length`. Every brief carries the full dossier shape the app expects.

| File | Tests | Cases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `room.jsonl` | The five editors' notes. Each draft carries 4 to 6 planted features with the editor ids expected to catch them. | 8 genres, including Morgan Vale's "Salt Roads". |
| `rubric.jsonl` | Rubric grading. Four topics, each with a strong and a weak draft sharing one brief. Weak drafts are fluent but generic, padded, hedged and off-goal; `weaknesses` lists what was planted. | 8 |
| `rewrite.jsonl` | Persona rewrites at sentence and paragraph level. `original` is the passage to rewrite, `problem` says what is wrong, `mustPreserve` lists facts a faithful rewrite keeps. All five personas appear. | 8 |
| `dossier.jsonl` | Drift from the brief: wrong audience register, goal never addressed, constraints broken (banned topics, word limits, forbidden figures), tone mismatch. `drifts` name the brief field each passage violates. | 4 |

## Plant kinds (`room.jsonl`)

`unsupported-claim`, `factual-error` (scholar), `weak-argument` (devil), `strong-passage` (angel), `bloat`, `repetition` (editor), `audience-gap`, `buried-lede` (reader, sometimes editor). `expectedEditors` is the set of editor ids a good run should see raise the passage; other editors may also comment.

## Verbatim rule

Every `passage`, `original`, `mustPreserve` entry and drift `passage` is an exact, character-for-character substring that appears exactly once in its `draftText` (`mustPreserve` entries appear once in `original`). Passages use straight quotes and plain ASCII punctuation. Edit a draft and you must re-check its passages.

const feature = `The pharmacy on Mill Street closes at six, and by a quarter to, on the Tuesday I was there, nine people were waiting. Two had come from Hallam Cross, eleven miles east, where the chemist shut in March. One had driven forty minutes from the other side of the reservoir because her husband's blood thinner was out of stock everywhere closer. A man in a council fleece was there for nothing at all. He had come in, he told me, because the pharmacist knows his mother's medication better than his mother does, and he wanted to ask whether the new tablets were the reason she had stopped sleeping.

Dunmore Pharmacy is the last independent chemist in a valley that had six when its owner, Rhona Petrie, bought it in 1998. She is sixty-one. Her lease runs out in fourteen months and she has not yet decided whether to renew it. If she does not, the nearest pharmacy for the eleven thousand people who live between the reservoir and the county line will be the supermarket counter in Breckonhead, which is a twenty-two mile drive and does not open on Sundays.

This is not a story about one shop. Across the country, community pharmacies have been closing at a rate of roughly two a week since 2016, and the closures are not evenly spread. They fall on the places that were already thin: the valleys, the coastal strips, the ex-industrial towns where the high street is half shutters. The reasons are not mysterious, and Petrie can list them without pausing. The dispensing fee the health service pays her per prescription has fallen in real terms for a decade. The wholesale price of common generics swings so wildly that she sometimes dispenses at a loss. And the work that is not dispensing, the work the man in the council fleece came in for, is not paid at all.

I spent four days in Dunmore in September. I wanted to understand what a pharmacy actually does for a town like this, beyond handing over boxes, and what the town stands to lose if the shutters come down on Mill Street too.

The first thing to say is that the handing over of boxes is itself more than it looks. Petrie dispenses about four hundred and twenty prescriptions a day, which is a high number for a single-pharmacist shop. Each one is checked against the patient's record for interactions, for duplicated therapy, for the dose that a locum doctor at the out-of-hours service wrote at two in the morning without seeing the notes. On the Tuesday I watched her catch three. One was a repeat prescription for a blood pressure drug that had been stopped at a hospital discharge the week before. The discharge letter had not reached the surgery. It had reached Petrie, because the patient's daughter had brought it in.

"The system assumes the information moves on its own," Petrie said. "It doesn't. It moves because somebody's daughter puts it in her handbag."

The second thing a pharmacy does is absorb what the rest of the health service cannot. The surgery in Dunmore has two general practitioners for a list of nine thousand. The wait for a routine appointment is three weeks. The pharmacy has no appointments and no wait longer than the queue, and so it has become, by default, the place people go first. Petrie and her two counter staff field somewhere between sixty and ninety questions a day that are not about a prescription. Is this rash something. Can I take this with that. My father is confused this morning and I do not know whether it is the infection or the new tablets. Some of these she answers. Some she sends on. A few, over the years, she has sent straight to hospital, and at least two of those people, she believes, would otherwise have died.

The health service does, in theory, pay for some of this. There is a scheme under which a surgery can refer a patient with a minor ailment to the pharmacy and the pharmacy is paid a small fee for the consultation. Petrie signed up to it in its first year. In the twelve months to August she was paid for forty-one such consultations. She estimates she did two thousand.

The money is the heart of it, and it is worth being precise about how it works, because the way it works explains the closures better than any single policy decision. A community pharmacy earns its living in three ways. It is paid a fixed fee for every item it dispenses. It is reimbursed for the cost of the drug itself, at a price set centrally each month. And it keeps whatever it can make on the shop floor, from the toothpaste and the sun cream and the hot water bottles. In a town like Dunmore the shop floor barely covers the heating.

The dispensing fee has been the quiet problem. It was set at a level in 2005 that, adjusted for inflation, would be worth nearly double what the fee is today, and it has been frozen or cut in cash terms in eight of the last ten years. The reimbursement price is the loud one. It is meant to track what pharmacies actually pay wholesalers, but it is set in arrears, and when a generic goes short, as they do now with a regularity that would have been unthinkable a decade ago, the wholesale price can triple in a fortnight while the reimbursement price stays where it was. Petrie showed me her invoice for a common antidepressant in June. She had paid eleven pounds forty a pack. She had been reimbursed three pounds ten. She dispensed sixty packs that month.

There is a mechanism for this. A pharmacy can apply for a concession price when a drug goes short, and the department publishes a list of concessions each month. The list in June ran to a hundred and forty lines. The antidepressant was not on it until August.
